title: Retirement income: AMP backs contested pension boost offering
full_text:
Asset manager AMP has defended retirement products engineered to artificially trim superannuation balances to enable retirees to max out their age pension entitlements ahead of an anticipated government crackdown.
AMP retirement director Ben Hillier told The Australian Financial Review Super and Wealth Summit the so-called innovative retirement income streams (IRIS), such as its Lifetime Boost product, increased confidence and spending in retirement.
Hillier said there was evidence that Lifetime Boost customers spent "significantly more in retirement" and the ability of all retirees to move $2.1 million into retirement phase tax-free was a "much more significant incentive" than using an IRIS product to qualify for a part age pension. He added that the product was not used exclusively by clients from the "top end of town".
"About 60 per cent of these people have balances less than $500,000. These are everyday Australians taking advantage of the incentives which the government, I think, has wisely put in place to incentivise consumption of superannuation," he said.
He made the comments as the broader wealth management sector prepared for a Treasury consultation that industry figures feared would look to dramatically curb the products.
Similar IRIS products - which optimise traditional retirement rules by guaranteeing income for life while unlocking favourable pension means-test concessions - were also offered by AMP's retail super rivals, MLC and Colonial First State.
Only 60 per cent of the gross income received from a boost product was counted as assessable income by Centrelink. AMP promoted that retirees using them could receive $100,000 more in the first 10 years of retirement.
But critics and competitors rounded on the products, saying that they encouraged people to double-dip on the age pension at a cost to taxpayers.
Many of the benefits in the products were not portable, meaning if members switched funds they would lose the accrued advantages, which discouraged them from changing superannuation provider.
Hillier, however, argued the government explicitly encouraged the development of such products through measures like the retirement income covenant and recent best practice principles in retirement.
Both aimed to solve the longstanding issue of retirees not drawing down enough of their super, instead only making withdrawals at a minimal level and dying with most of their wealth intact.
"For me, there's very little residual debate about the value of these things," he said.
MLC Expand chief executive Liz McCarthy said the company had "great success" with its IRIS product.
"We were asked to innovate, to do something different for Australians, and we've done that," said McCarthy, who described the products as giving members choice about how they invested their super.
Hillier said that while take-up of such products had been "really small", the take-up of annuity products in the UK was about 30 per cent and "that was the level we should be aspiring to" for lifetime income products in Australia.
"Our take-up rates in Australia [of annuities] are 1 or 2 per cent. With Lifetime Boost at AMP, we're getting take-up rates of about 12 per cent of our members," he said.
Nine Entertainment Co.
